Plus: Nvidia aftershocks | Thursday, November 12, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Markets
By Emily Peck and Matt Phillips · Nov 12, 2026

👋 Welcome back! We took a day off, and, well, a bubble just burst.

  • It's not THE bubble — the multitrillion-dollar dash to build out an AI world — but it's the bubble of invulnerability that Silicon Valley's leaders had wrapped themselves in until now. And that may be unsettling. Superstar Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is in hot water, and Wall Street is not happy.
  • We get into it below.

📉 This morning, stock futures are down slightly after last night's reporting that Nvidia's board is meeting to discuss Huang's ouster.

  • Marvell and Micron Technology are down in the premarket — after the semiconductor sector saw a bounce up on yesterday. All eyes will be on the AI trade today.

Let's get into it! In 1,081 words, a 4-minute read.

 
 
1 big thing: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Huang's apparent fall from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the entire AI ecosystem that he did much to create.

Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia.

  • Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy.

Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported yesterday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

  • The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang.
  • Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session.
  • This morning, the shares were down 7.8% in premarket trading at our deadline.

Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years.

  • The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers.
  • Chipmakers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down almost 30% from their recent high through yesterday's close, vaporizing about $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth.
  • There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a new report on the investment cycle.
  • "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness."

Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost more than $600 billion in market value.

Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios.

  • With a market capitalization of roughly $4.19 trillion — through yesterday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100.

Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is.

  • It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers.
  • It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power.
  • That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds.
  • For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that has seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI.

Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers.

  • In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day.

State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement.

  • Yesterday, the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research.
  • "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
  • Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day.

The bottom line: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis.

  • "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused. If — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions."
 
 
2. Huang's money-making machine
By Matt Phillips
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history.

  • From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet.

The big picture: He has been at the helm of the company since co-founding it in 1993.

The bottom line: Depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

3. Midterm mood swing
By Emily Peck
 
Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races.

  • The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics.

Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending.

  • Lately, it's looked more like a political measure.
